analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classified this binary as malware with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top SHAP features push toward cryptojacking. No counter-evidence appears in the list. The n-grams fall into three groups that fit the instruction mix of a hashing or mining routine. (1) Rotate/shift/add arithmetic: ADD ROR (+0.009624), ROL ADD (+0.009248), ADD ROL (+0.005493), ROL MOV (+0.005609), SHRD XOR (+0.007318), SHL NEG (+0.005617), SHL XCHG (+0.005850) and SUB ADC (+0.005476). This is the bit-mixing and multi-word arithmetic typical of cryptographic hash and PoW primitives. (2) SIMD bitwise/vector patterns: PXOR MOVAPS (+0.014490, the top feature), PXOR MOVUPS (+0.009634), MOVDQA PAND (+0.008400), PAND PXOR (+0.007511) and PADDQ MOVDQA (+0.005897). These suggest vectorized XOR/AND/add operations on 128-bit data, which are common in optimized mining kernels. MOVAPD DIVSD (+0.006137) is a floating-point pattern whose role is less clear. (3) Generic control-flow and stack patterns: ADD PUSH, POP LEA, PUSH RET, CALL RET, CALL PUSH and POP PUSH. These are common in all compiled code and are weak evidence individually, though their SHAP contributions (+0.006 to +0.011) still point toward malware. The strongest features are the rare SIMD and rotate/shift arithmetic n-grams, and their combination supports a high-confidence cryptojacking call. The evidence is limited to mnemonic n-grams. It contains no function names, API calls or network indicators, so the call rests on instruction-level statistical patterns plus the model's very confident output.

Generic stack/arithmetic sequence. Weak on its own, but it contributes toward the malware class in this model.
Unaligned-load variant of SIMD XOR handling. It reinforces the vectorized bitwise-processing pattern seen in rank 1.
Add combined with rotate-right is a classic ARX-style mixing step in hash and cipher rounds, consistent with PoW hashing.
Rotate-left followed by add is another ARX-style primitive, consistent with hash round functions.
Aligned 128-bit load followed by bitwise AND indicates masking in vectorized data processing, consistent with SIMD hash implementations.
Common function epilogue/address-computation pattern. Low specificity, but it contributes toward the malware class.
Back-to-back SIMD AND/XOR operations suggest bitwise logic of the kind used in hash compression functions.
Control-flow idiom that can indicate indirect transfers or unusual call/return handling. Ambiguous without more context.
Double-precision shift combined with XOR suggests multi-word bit manipulation, as in large-integer or hash arithmetic.
Very rare sequence (frequency 0.000001) that suggests an unusual structure such as tiny stub functions. Its link to mining is indirect.
Common calling-convention pattern. Low specificity, but it adds to the malware score.
Generic register save/restore pattern. Weak individually.
Floating-point double-precision move and divide. It is unusual alongside the integer/SIMD pattern and its role is unclear, but it was rare and still influential.
64-bit packed addition with an aligned move indicates vectorized arithmetic on 128-bit lanes, consistent with SIMD hash computation.
Very rare shift/exchange combination that may reflect low-level bit manipulation or byte-swapping, which fits hashing routines.

Rotation followed by a move indicates rotation-based mixing, consistent with the other rotate n-grams.
Add then rotate-left is another ARX-style round pattern that supports the hashing interpretation.
Subtract with add-with-carry indicates multi-precision arithmetic, which appears in big-integer and cryptographic computations.

analysis.recommended_action: Treat the sample as likely cryptojacking malware and prioritize it for deeper analysis. Disassemble the functions containing the SIMD (PXOR/PAND/PADDQ) and rotate/add n-grams to confirm a hash or PoW loop, such as a mining algorithm. Then run it in a sandbox to observe CPU usage, network connections to mining pools and persistence behavior, and extract any configuration data (pool addresses, wallets).
